newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour hides split over EMU.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour hides split over EMU.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair's new-style management of the Labour party has ensured a show of public unity over policy that has left Britain's ruling Conservatives bitterly frustrated.

The Labour achievement which has caused most anguish among Conservative strategists, preparing for a highly charged conference of their own next week, is Blair's success in containing genuine differences over a European single currency.

By focussing Labour's attacks and media attention on Prime Minister John Major's attempts to halt his party's almost suicidal squabbling over Europe, Blair has managed to to forge a broad consensus over policy.
This has transformed what was once as wide a divide as in the Conservative party into mere differences over strategy.

Leading figures from foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook, the most powerful left-winger in Blair's team, to economics spokesman Gordon Brown, are broadly in favour of a single European currency on economic grounds.

Arguing the Conservative row about sovereignty is sterile since a country's monetary sovereignty is already compromised in a world of rapid cross-border financial transactions, they agree a single currency would be good for business.

Even the unions are on board. John Monks, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, told a conference fringe meeting this week: "We are really keen to take a decision in the interests of growth...we are in favour of going forward."
The standard Labour position on Europe and the single currency was set out once again this week by Blair.
"Let me make it plain, I will not scrap Britain's veto in Europe," he said in his keynote speech.
"Our options on a single currency should remain open, to be determined according to our national interest. Any change will only come with the full consent of the people."
But as always in politics, the devil is in the detail.

Blair has pledged that a decision will be based on whether there is real rather than purely monetary convergence -- fundamentally whether Britain can compete equally with its European partners without losing jobs.
The "consent of the people" pledged by Blair would probably be via a referendum.

Senior Labour sources, dismissing a Times report that the leadership was edging towards a decision on strategy as an attempt to bounce the party into a quick pre-election choice, said this debate over tactics continues.
The question is whether Blair should include a clear commitment in the manifesto for the forthcoming election.
Right-wingers like Brown believe such a step is advisable.

Brown, aides said, agrees with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, who outraged so-called Eurosceptics in his Conservative party by saying that it would be "pathetic" to stay out of a single currency only to join later.

But with a decision needed on whether to join the first wave of a single currency in Spring 1998, there would be little time for a new Labour administration to prepare a referendum if the election is held at the last possible date next year, May.

There would also be a strong chance, especially if Conservative opponents keep up their campaign, the referendum could be lost, severely damaging Britain's standing in the European Union and its options of joining the currency later.
But left-wingers like Cook believe it would be foolish to make a commitment when the overall effect of a single currency, particularly on jobs, is still not clear.
Left-wingers believe a Labour government would have support from other left-leaning governments in Europe in ensuring that some kind of jobs programme was developed alongside the single currency.

But they are concerned that Major's paralysis in Europe as a result of his party's divisions could allow France and Germany to forge ahead, leaving little scope or time for a Labour government in Britain to make its mark.
